chapter_note.about: A queue is a line: items join at the rear and leave from the front, so the oldest item always goes first. This chapter covers queue tracing, the circular array and linked-list implementations, the deque, how queues and stacks can be built from each other, how to add up the cost of a whole sequence of operations, and where queues are used in BFS and scheduling. GATE asks short traces and costing questions. The habit that helps most is drawing the structure after every operation and checking which end each operation touches.
chapter_note.simple: A queue is the line at a ticket counter: you join at the back, and the person who has waited longest is served first. A circular queue is a ring of chairs where freed chairs get reused, a linked queue is a chain of carriages with a note at each end, and a deque is a line with a door at both ends. You can imitate a queue with two piles of plates, or a pile with two queues, if you move people between them carefully. When a question asks about cost, add up the whole sequence: each person leaves at most once, which keeps the total small.

cards.title: FIFO, enqueue and dequeue
cards.simple: Think of the line at a ticket counter. People join at the back, and the person at the front is served first. Nobody cuts in and nobody leaves from the middle. A queue in a program is that line. Enqueue adds an item at the rear, dequeue removes the item at the front, so items leave in the same order they arrived. In exam words: a queue is FIFO (first in, first out), with enqueue at the rear and dequeue at the front.
cards.idea: A queue is a list with two ends that have different jobs. New items join at the **rear** and leave from the **front**. The item that has waited longest always leaves first, which is the **FIFO** rule: first in, first out.
cards.definition:
A queue supports:

- `enqueue(x)`: add `x` at the rear.
- `dequeue()`: remove and return the front item.
- `front()` (or `peek()`): return the front item without removing it.

Order of removal equals order of insertion. Dequeue on an empty queue is **underflow**. Each operation is O(1) in a good implementation.
cards.intuition_full: A stack reverses order; a queue keeps it. That is the whole difference, and it is why queues model fairness: print jobs, ticket lines, tasks waiting for the CPU. To trace a queue, write the items in a row, mark the front on the left and the rear on the right, and update the row after every operation. Enqueue appends on the right; dequeue deletes on the left. Because items never overtake each other, the k-th item to be dequeued is the k-th one enqueued. That gives a quick check: the sequence of dequeued values is always a prefix of the sequence of enqueued values (when no value is enqueued from elsewhere). If a program dequeues a value and enqueues it again, it moves from front to rear: the queue rotates.

examples.setup: An empty queue gets `enqueue(4), enqueue(9), enqueue(1), dequeue(), enqueue(7), dequeue(), dequeue()`. What values come out, and what is left in the queue?
steps: `enqueue(4)`, `enqueue(9)`, `enqueue(1)`: items join at the rear. Queue (front to rear): [4, 9, 1].
`dequeue()` removes the front item, 4. The queue is [9, 1].
`enqueue(7)` adds at the rear: [9, 1, 7].
`dequeue()` removes the front, 9. The queue is [1, 7].
`dequeue()` removes the front, 1. The queue is [7].
Values out: 4, 9, 1. Left: [7], with 7 at the front.
examples.answer: The values come out as 4, 9, 1 and the queue is [7]. Items leave in the order they arrived: first in, first out.

examples.setup: A queue starts as [3, 7] (front on the left). Repeat 3 times: `x = dequeue(); y = front(); enqueue(x + y)`. Give the final queue and the sum of the three dequeued values. (`front()` only reads the front item.)
steps: Round 1: dequeue 3, the queue is [7]. `front()` reads 7 without removing it. Enqueue 3 + 7 = 10: [7, 10].
Round 2: dequeue 7, the queue is [10]. `front()` is 10. Enqueue 7 + 10 = 17: [10, 17].
Round 3: dequeue 10, the queue is [17]. `front()` is 17. Enqueue 10 + 17 = 27: [17, 27].
Dequeued values: 3 + 7 + 10 = 20.
examples.answer: The final queue is [17, 27] and the dequeued sum is 20. `front()` reads, `dequeue()` removes; mixing them up shifts every number.

examples.setup: On an empty queue: `enqueue(1), enqueue(2), dequeue(), dequeue(), dequeue(), enqueue(3)`. The third `dequeue` hits an empty queue. What does the queue hold at the end?
steps: `enqueue(1)`, `enqueue(2)`: [1, 2].
Two `dequeue` calls remove 1 and 2. The queue is empty.
The third `dequeue` is an underflow error. It removes nothing and changes nothing.
`enqueue(3)` adds to the empty queue: [3].
examples.answer: The queue holds [3]. An underflow does not damage the structure, and the next enqueue works normally.

cards.title: Circular array queue
cards.simple: Imagine a ring-shaped waiting area with 6 numbered chairs. When the person at the front is called, their chair becomes free again. New people can sit there, even though it is 'behind' the line, because after chair 5 the ring comes back to chair 0. To tell a completely full ring from a completely empty one, one chair is always left empty. In exam words: a circular array queue wraps its indices with mod n; with one slot kept empty, empty is `front == rear` and full is `(rear + 1) mod n == front`.
cards.idea: A plain array queue wastes the cells at the front after dequeues. A **circular** queue fixes this by wrapping indices around: after the last cell comes cell 0 again. It needs two indices, `front` and `rear`, and a way to tell full from empty.
cards.definition:
For an array of size `n`, with `front` the first item and `rear` the next free slot:

- `enqueue`: `A[rear] = x; rear = (rear + 1) mod n`.
- `dequeue`: `x = A[front]; front = (front + 1) mod n`.
- Empty: `front == rear`.
- Full (one cell kept empty): `(rear + 1) mod n == front`, so capacity is `n - 1`.
- Number of items: `(rear - front + n) mod n`.

With a separate `count` variable, all `n` cells can be used.
cards.intuition_full: Both indices only move forward, and the `mod n` turns the line into a ring. The trouble is that a full ring and an empty ring look the same: both have `front == rear`, because `rear` has gone all the way round. There are two standard fixes. One is to stop one step early, so that the full ring has `rear` just behind `front`. This sacrifices one cell and gives the tests above. The other is to keep a count. The number-of-items formula `(rear - front + n) mod n` is subtraction on a ring: `+ n` removes negative results and `mod n` removes the full turn. When a GATE question changes the convention (for example `rear` as the last item and not the next free slot), the tests shift by one, so check the convention in the question before writing any formula.

examples.setup: A circular queue uses an array of 6 cells. `front` is the index of the first item and `rear` is the next free slot; both start at 0. One cell is kept empty to tell full from empty. Do: enqueue A, B, C, D, E; dequeue twice; enqueue F, G. Where do `front` and `rear` end, and is the queue full?
steps: Empty when `front == rear`. Full when `(rear + 1) mod 6 == front`. Start: `front = 0`, `rear = 0`.
Enqueue A to E stores them at indices 0 to 4. `rear` moves to 5. Now `(5 + 1) mod 6 = 0 = front`, so the queue is full with 5 items. Capacity is n - 1 = 5.
Two dequeues remove A and B. `front` moves to 2.
Enqueue F goes to index 5. `rear = (5 + 1) mod 6 = 0`: it wraps to the start of the array.
Enqueue G goes to index 0. `rear = 1`. Now `(1 + 1) mod 6 = 2 = front`: full again.
Items from front to rear are C, D, E, F, G. Count = `(rear - front + 6) mod 6 = (1 - 2 + 6) mod 6 = 5`.
examples.answer: `front = 2`, `rear = 1`, and the queue is full with 5 items. The wrap-around uses the cells freed by the dequeues.

examples.setup: A circular queue in an array of 12 cells keeps one cell unused. `front = 9` and `rear = 4`, where `rear` is the next free slot. How many items are in the queue, which indices hold them, and how many more can be enqueued?
steps: Count = `(rear - front + n) mod n = (4 - 9 + 12) mod 12 = 7`.
Items start at index 9 and run 9, 10, 11, then wrap to 0, 1, 2, 3. That is 7 cells.
Capacity is `n - 1 = 11`, so 11 - 7 = 4 more items fit.
Check: after 4 more enqueues `rear = 8`, and `(8 + 1) mod 12 = 9 = front`: full.
examples.answer: 7 items at indices 9, 10, 11, 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4 more can be enqueued. Plain subtraction `rear - front = -5` is wrong because the queue wraps.

examples.setup: A circular queue of size 4 stores a separate counter `count` instead of leaving a cell empty. It enqueues 4 items. What are `front`, `rear`, and the full and empty tests?
steps: Start: `front = 0`, `rear = 0` (next free slot), `count = 0`.
After 4 enqueues, indices 0 to 3 are filled and `rear = 4 mod 4 = 0`. So `rear == front` while the queue is full.
Because `front == rear` is now ambiguous, the tests use the counter: empty when `count == 0`, full when `count == 4`.
All 4 cells are usable, so capacity is `n`, not `n - 1`.
examples.answer: With a counter the capacity is 4, and `front == rear` no longer tells full from empty. Without a counter, one cell must stay empty.

cards.why: Circular queues test the boundary conditions. In GATE: the full and empty conditions, the number of items from `front` and `rear`, and the capacity with one cell sacrificed (2012 CS Q35, 2016 CS1 Q10).
how: Read the convention: is `rear` the last item or the next free slot?
Empty is `front == rear`; full is `(rear + 1) mod n == front` (one cell unused).
Items = `(rear - front + n) mod n`; capacity = `n - 1`.
Always apply `mod n` after incrementing an index.
cards.mistake: Forgetting the wrap or using `rear - front` directly. In an array of 12 with `front = 9` and `rear = 4`, the difference is -5, but the queue holds 7 items. Always add `n` and take mod `n`. Also note: with one cell left empty, an array of size n holds only n - 1 items.
edge_cases: `rear` at the last index moves to 0 on the next enqueue.
Capacity is `n - 1` without a counter, `n` with one.
Different conventions (rear = last item) shift full/empty tests by one.
A single item: `rear = front + 1` (mod n).

cards.title: Linked-list queue
cards.simple: Think of a train where each carriage only knows which carriage is directly behind it. To serve the passenger in the first carriage, you need to know where the train starts. To add a passenger at the back, you need to know where the train ends. So the station keeps two notes: one pointing at the first carriage (head) and one pointing at the last (tail). Without the tail note you would walk the whole train every time. In exam words: a linked-list queue keeps head and tail pointers; enqueue at the tail and dequeue at the head are both O(1), and dequeue at the tail of a singly linked list is Theta(n).
cards.idea: A queue can be a linked list instead of an array, with no size limit and no wasted cells. You keep a pointer to the first node (`head`) and one to the last node (`tail`). New items go after the tail, and items leave from the head.
cards.definition:
Singly linked queue with `head` and `tail`:

- `enqueue(x)`: new node `n`. If empty then `head = tail = n`; else `tail.next = n; tail = n`.
- `dequeue()`: `x = head.value; head = head.next`; if `head` is now NULL then `tail = NULL`. Return `x`.

Both are O(1). Without a `tail` pointer, enqueue costs Theta(n) because you must walk to the end.

Circular variant: keep one pointer `rear` to the last node; the front is `rear.next`.
cards.intuition_full: The choice of ends matters because a singly linked node knows only its successor. Adding after a known node is easy, and removing the first node is easy: both use only the pointer we hold. Removing the last node is hard, because we need its predecessor to make that predecessor the new last node, and nothing points backwards. So the queue must remove at the end that is cheap to remove (the head) and add at the end that is cheap to add (the tail, via a tail pointer). The special case is a one-node queue: removing it empties the queue, so `tail` must follow `head` to NULL. A circular list reaches both ends with one pointer: if `rear` points at the last node, `rear.next` is the first node.

examples.setup: A queue is a singly linked list with `head` and `tail` pointers; enqueue adds at the tail and dequeue removes at the head. Starting empty, do `enqueue(5), enqueue(8), enqueue(2), dequeue(), dequeue(), dequeue()`. Show where `head` and `tail` point after each step.
steps: Empty queue: `head = tail = NULL`. `enqueue(5)` creates a node. Both `head` and `tail` point at it.
`enqueue(8)`: `tail.next = new node; tail = new node`. No walking along the list. Now 5 → 8, `tail` at 8.
`enqueue(2)`: the same two assignments. List 5 → 8 → 2, `head` at 5, `tail` at 2.
`dequeue()`: return `head.value` (5), then `head = head.next`. The 5 node is unlinked and `head` is at 8.
`dequeue()` returns 8 and `head` moves to 2. The last `dequeue()` returns 2 and `head` becomes NULL. Now the queue is empty, so `tail` must also be set to NULL.
examples.answer: Items come out as 5, 8, 2, and at the end `head` and `tail` are both NULL. Each operation changes two pointers at most: O(1).

examples.setup: A queue is stored as a singly linked list with a `head` and a `tail` pointer. Choice A: enqueue at the head, dequeue at the tail. Choice B: enqueue at the tail, dequeue at the head. Which choice gives O(1) for both operations?
steps: Choice A: enqueue at the head is O(1): new node, `new.next = head`, `head = new`.
Choice A: dequeue at the tail needs the node **before** the tail so that its `next` can be cleared. A singly linked node cannot go backwards, so we walk from the head: Theta(n).
Choice B: enqueue at the tail is `tail.next = new; tail = new`: O(1).
Choice B: dequeue at the head is `head = head.next`: O(1).
examples.answer: Choice B. Removing at the tail of a singly linked list costs Theta(n), because the predecessor must be found by walking. A circular list with one pointer to the **rear** also works: front = `rear.next`.

examples.setup: A queue holds exactly one node, 7, with `head = tail = node7`. The code for `dequeue` is `x = head.value; head = head.next; return x` and it never touches `tail`. After this dequeue, `enqueue(9)` runs `tail.next = new; tail = new`. What goes wrong?
steps: After the dequeue, `head = node7.next = NULL`. The queue should be empty, but `tail` still points at the old node 7.
`enqueue(9)` does `tail.next = new`: it attaches the new node to the removed node 7. `tail = new`.
`head` is still NULL, so the queue looks empty even though a node exists. The new item is lost.
Fix: in `dequeue`, if `head` becomes NULL, also set `tail = NULL`, and in `enqueue` set `head = tail = new` when the queue is empty.
examples.answer: The enqueued 9 is unreachable from `head`. The last-item dequeue must reset `tail`; the empty-queue case needs its own handling.

cards.why: Linked-list queue costs are a recurring theory question. In GATE: complexity of enqueue and dequeue with and without a tail pointer, and which end to use (2017 CS2 Q13, 2018 CS Q13, 2004 CS Q36).
how: Ask: which end gets insertions, which end gets deletions?
Insert after a known node (tail) and delete the first node (head): O(1) each.
Deleting the last node needs the predecessor: Theta(n) in a singly linked list.
Handle the one-node and empty cases: set both pointers.
cards.mistake: Believing that a tail pointer makes the removal at the tail O(1). A tail pointer gives O(1) **insertion** at the tail, but deleting the tail node still needs its predecessor, which costs Theta(n) in a singly linked list. A doubly linked list can do it in O(1).
edge_cases: Empty queue: `head = tail = NULL`.
Last item removed: also reset `tail` to NULL.
Circular list with only `rear`: enqueue and dequeue are both O(1).
Head-only list with enqueue at the end: enqueue is Theta(n).

cards.what_full:
A queue can be a linked list instead of an array, with no size limit and no wasted cells. You keep a pointer to the first node (`head`) and one to the last node (`tail`). New items go after the tail, and items leave from the head.

Singly linked queue with `head` and `tail`:

- `enqueue(x)`: new node `n`. If empty then `head = tail = n`; else `tail.next = n; tail = n`.
- `dequeue()`: `x = head.value; head = head.next`; if `head` is now NULL then `tail = NULL`. Return `x`.

Both are O(1). Without a `tail` pointer, enqueue costs Theta(n) because you must walk to the end.

Circular variant: keep one pointer `rear` to the last node; the front is `rear.next`.

**Worked example.** A queue is a singly linked list with `head` and `tail` pointers; enqueue adds at the tail and dequeue removes at the head. Starting empty, do `enqueue(5), enqueue(8), enqueue(2), dequeue(), dequeue(), dequeue()`. Show where `head` and `tail` point after each step.

1. Empty queue: `head = tail = NULL`. `enqueue(5)` creates a node. Both `head` and `tail` point at it.
2. `enqueue(8)`: `tail.next = new node; tail = new node`. No walking along the list. Now 5 → 8, `tail` at 8.
3. `enqueue(2)`: the same two assignments. List 5 → 8 → 2, `head` at 5, `tail` at 2.
4. `dequeue()`: return `head.value` (5), then `head = head.next`. The 5 node is unlinked and `head` is at 8.
5. `dequeue()` returns 8 and `head` moves to 2. The last `dequeue()` returns 2 and `head` becomes NULL. Now the queue is empty, so `tail` must also be set to NULL.

**Answer:** Items come out as 5, 8, 2, and at the end `head` and `tail` are both NULL. Each operation changes two pointers at most: O(1).

cards.title: Deque
cards.simple: A deque (say 'deck') is a queue with a door at both ends. You can join or leave from the front or from the back. If you always join at one end and leave at the other, it is an ordinary line. If you join and leave at the same end, it is a pile of plates where the last one in leaves first. In exam words: a deque allows insert and remove at both ends; with insertLast and removeLast it behaves as a stack, and with insertLast and removeFirst it behaves as a queue.
cards.idea: A **deque** (double-ended queue) generalises both stack and queue. It has four main operations, one for each end and each direction. All four take O(1) in a standard implementation (doubly linked list or circular array).
cards.definition:
A deque supports:

- `insertFirst(x)` and `insertLast(x)`: add at the front or the rear.
- `removeFirst()` and `removeLast()`: remove and return the front or the rear item.
- Optional `first()` and `last()` to read the ends.

Stack = use only one end. Queue = insert at one end and remove at the other. Python: `append`, `appendleft`, `pop`, `popleft`.
cards.intuition_full: A stack touches one end; a queue touches both ends but each end has one job. A deque removes the job restrictions. It is helpful when an algorithm needs to take from both sides: sliding window problems, palindromes, undo and redo. Tracing is the same as before, but with a row where both ends are active. Write the row, and for each operation say 'front' or 'rear' before you change anything. The two classic mistakes are mixing up the two ends and forgetting that `removeLast` returns the item most recently inserted at the rear. Also note that in a singly linked list `removeLast` is slow; deques use doubly linked nodes or a circular array to keep all four operations O(1).

examples.setup: A deque starts empty. Operations: `insertFirst(7), insertFirst(1), insertLast(5), removeLast(), insertLast(9), removeFirst(), removeLast()`. What does each remove return, and what is left?
steps: `insertFirst(7)`: the deque is [7].
`insertFirst(1)` puts 1 at the front: [1, 7].
`insertLast(5)` puts 5 at the rear: [1, 7, 5].
`removeLast()` removes the rear item and returns 5: [1, 7].
`insertLast(9)`: [1, 7, 9].
`removeFirst()` removes the front item and returns 1: [7, 9].
`removeLast()` returns 9: [7].
examples.answer: The removes return 5, 1, 9 and the deque is [7]. Each end acts independently, and an item inserted at one end can be removed from either.

cards.title: Queue from stacks, stack from queues
cards.simple: Imagine you only own queues, but you need a stack, where the newest item comes out first. The newest item is at the back of the queue, but a queue only lets you take from the front. So you move everyone else into a second queue, take the last person, and then the two queues swap jobs. It works, but it is slow at one end. In exam words: a stack from two queues makes push or pop O(n); a queue from two stacks pours between them; a stack with a reverse operation can also act as a queue.
cards.idea: Each structure can imitate the other by moving items between two containers so that the order flips. Two queues build a stack by making the newest item reach the front, at O(n) cost per push or per pop. Two stacks build a queue by pouring one into the other, which reverses the order (that case is traced in the stacks chapter).
cards.definition:
- **Stack from two queues, costly pop:** `push(x)`: enqueue on Q1. `pop()`: move all but the last item of Q1 to Q2, dequeue the last as the result, swap Q1 and Q2.
- **Stack from two queues, costly push:** `push(x)`: enqueue on Q2, then move all of Q1 behind it, swap Q1 and Q2. `pop()`: dequeue from Q1.
- **Queue from two stacks:** push on S1; to dequeue, pour S1 into S2 only if S2 is empty, then pop S2.
- **Queue from one stack and REVERSE:** enqueue is REVERSE, PUSH, REVERSE; dequeue is POP.
cards.intuition_full: The core problem is that one structure hides the item the other one needs. A queue hides its newest item at the rear; a stack hides its oldest item at the bottom. To reach a hidden item you must move the items in front of it somewhere else. Moving them through a second container keeps their order (queue to queue) or reverses it (stack to stack), and that is exactly what you design for. The cost is proportional to the number of items moved, so one operation becomes O(n) while the other stays O(1). Counting operations then reduces to summing a series: with sizes 1 to n the cost is 1 + 3 + 5 + ... = n^2. In the stack-to-stack case the reversal happens twice and each item is moved only once per pour, so the amortised cost is O(1).

examples.setup: A stack is built from two queues. `push(x)` enqueues `x` on the active queue. `pop()` moves all but the last item to the spare queue, dequeues the last item as the result, and then the two queues swap roles. Operations: `push 4, push 7, push 2, pop, push 9, pop, pop`. What do the pops return, and how many queue operations (each enqueue and each dequeue counts 1) are used?
steps: Three pushes enqueue 4, 7, 2 on the active queue: [4, 7, 2]. The newest item, 2, sits at the rear.
`pop()`: a queue removes only from the front, so move 4 and 7 to the spare queue (2 operations each). Active [2], spare [4, 7].
Dequeue 2 and return it (1 operation). The queues swap roles: active [4, 7], spare empty.
`push 9` enqueues on the active queue: [4, 7, 9].
`pop()`: move 4 and 7 across, dequeue 9 and return it. After the swap the active queue is [4, 7].
`pop()`: move 4 across (2 operations), dequeue 7 and return it (1). The active queue is [4].
Pops returned 2, 9, 7. Operation count: 4 enqueues for the pushes, plus 5 + 5 + 3 for the three pops, is 17.
examples.answer: The pops return 2, 9, 7 (newest first, as a stack should), using 17 queue operations. Here push is O(1) and pop is O(n).

examples.setup: Same stack-from-two-queues design (cheap push, costly pop). 5 pushes (1 to 5) are followed by 5 pops. How many queue operations are used, and in what order do the pops return values?
steps: The 5 pushes cost 5 operations, one enqueue each.
A pop on a stack of size k moves k - 1 items (2 operations each) and dequeues one: 2(k - 1) + 1 = 2k - 1 operations.
The pops happen at sizes 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, costing 9 + 7 + 5 + 3 + 1 = 25.
Total = 5 + 25 = 30. The pops return 5, 4, 3, 2, 1.
examples.answer: 30 operations; pops return 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. In general n pushes and n pops cost n + n^2 = Theta(n^2) with this design.

examples.setup: A queue can also be built from **one** stack plus an O(n) `REVERSE` operation: `enqueue(x)` does REVERSE, then PUSH x, then REVERSE; `dequeue()` is POP. Enqueue 1, 2, 3 and then dequeue. What comes out?

`enqueue(2)`: REVERSE [1] is [1], PUSH 2 gives [1, 2] (2 on top), REVERSE gives [2, 1] (1 on top).
`enqueue(3)`: REVERSE [2, 1] gives [1, 2], PUSH 3 gives [1, 2, 3], REVERSE gives [3, 2, 1] (1 on top).
`dequeue()` is POP: the top is 1, the oldest item.
examples.answer: It returns 1. The REVERSE before the push puts the old items on the right way up, and the reverse after restores them with the oldest on top. Enqueue costs O(n), dequeue O(1).

cards.title: Cost of an operation sequence
cards.simple: If a line of 100 people had to shuffle one step forward every time the first person was served, serving everyone would take about 100 x 100 / 2 steps. If instead a pointer moves to the next person, serving takes 100 steps. One operation can look cheap and still be costly when repeated, or look expensive and be cheap in total. So add up a whole sequence. In exam words: the total cost of n operations matters; each item is dequeued at most once, so n queue operations cost Theta(n), while n calls to list.pop(0) cost Theta(n^2).
cards.idea: The cost of one operation is not the whole story. Ask instead: what is the total cost of a sequence of `n` operations? Sometimes one operation is expensive, but it can only be expensive because many cheap operations happened before it. Then the total is small, and we say the **amortised** cost per operation is small.
cards.definition:
- **Worst-case cost** of one operation: the most it can take on one call.
- **Total cost** of a sequence: the sum of the costs of all operations in the sequence.
- **Amortised cost** = total cost / number of operations.

Queue facts:
- Array or linked queue with head and tail: enqueue and dequeue are O(1).
- Each item is removed at most once, so any `n` operations that include `MultiDequeue` cost Theta(n) in total.
- `list.pop(0)` shifts the whole list: Theta(n) per call.
cards.intuition_full: To bound a total, count what each item does during its life. A queued item is inserted once and removed at most once, so the total insertion cost plus the total removal cost is at most two units per item. A MultiDequeue can remove many items at once, but it cannot remove an item that is not there, and every item there was enqueued by an earlier operation. This accounting argument turns a scary worst case (k per call times n calls) into a small total (2n). The opposite example is `list.pop(0)`: here every call really does work proportional to the current length, and the sum of lengths is quadratic. The same thinking explains the head-only linked queue: the walk to the end is long every time, and there is no earlier saving to pay for it.

examples.setup: A Python list holds 5 items. You remove all of them one by one with `lst.pop(0)`. How many element moves (shifts) happen in total? Compare with `deque.popleft()` on a deque of the same 5 items.
steps: `pop(0)` removes the first element, and every element after it moves one place left. The list has 5 items, so 4 shifts.
Next `pop(0)`: 4 items remain, 3 shifts.
Next: 3 items remain, 2 shifts.
Next: 2 items remain, 1 shift.
Last: 1 item remains, 0 shifts. Total = 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 10.
A deque only moves its front pointer: 0 shifts. In general the list needs n(n - 1)/2 shifts for n removals.
examples.answer: 10 shifts for the list, 0 for the deque. n removals from the front of a list cost Theta(n^2); from a deque they cost Theta(n).

examples.setup: A queue supports `Enqueue`, `Dequeue` and `MultiDequeue(k)`, which removes up to `k` items. Each removal of one item costs 1, and an enqueue costs 1. A sequence of 10 operations on an initially empty queue has 6 enqueues and 4 MultiDequeue(4) calls. What is the largest possible total cost of the sequence?
steps: A single `MultiDequeue(4)` can remove up to 4 items, so it looks like 4 x 4 = 16 for four calls.
But only 6 items were ever enqueued, and each item can be removed at most once. So total removals are at most 6.
Total cost <= 6 (enqueues) + 6 (removals) = 12.
In general, n operations cost at most n enqueues + n removals = 2n = Theta(n).
examples.answer: At most 12 (not 16 or more). The worst single MultiDequeue is expensive, but the total over n operations is Theta(n), so the amortised cost per operation is constant.

examples.setup: A queue is a singly linked list with only a `head` pointer. `enqueue` walks from the head to the last node and appends there. How many nodes are visited (hops) in total for 6 enqueues on an initially empty queue?
steps: Enqueue 1: the list is empty, 0 hops.
Enqueue 2: walk past 1 node. Enqueue 3: 2 hops. Enqueue 4: 3. Enqueue 5: 4. Enqueue 6: 5.
With a tail pointer each enqueue is 1 step, so the total would be 6.
examples.answer: 15 hops. Without a tail pointer, n enqueues cost Theta(n^2). A single cheap operation repeated n times is not always cheap in total.

example.setup: A Python list holds 5 items. You remove all of them one by one with `lst.pop(0)`. How many element moves (shifts) happen in total? Compare with `deque.popleft()` on a deque of the same 5 items.
steps: `pop(0)` removes the first element, and every element after it moves one place left. The list has 5 items, so 4 shifts.
Next `pop(0)`: 4 items remain, 3 shifts.
Next: 3 items remain, 2 shifts.
Next: 2 items remain, 1 shift.
Last: 1 item remains, 0 shifts. Total = 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 10.
A deque only moves its front pointer: 0 shifts. In general the list needs n(n - 1)/2 shifts for n removals.
example.answer: 10 shifts for the list, 0 for the deque. n removals from the front of a list cost Theta(n^2); from a deque they cost Theta(n).

cards.what: The cost of one operation is not the whole story. Ask instead: what is the total cost of a sequence of `n` operations? Sometimes one operation is expensive, but it can only be expensive because many cheap operations happened before it. Then the total is small, and we say the **amortised** cost per operation is small.

cards.title: Stack and queue together
cards.simple: Picture a conveyor belt (queue) and a pile of boxes (stack) beside it. You can lift the front box off the belt and drop it on the pile, or lift the top box off the pile and put it at the back of the belt. If you move every box from belt to pile and then back, their order flips, because the pile gives back the last box first. These questions ask you to follow every box exactly. In exam words: items move between a queue and a stack; passing a whole queue through a stack reverses it; trace both containers after every operation.
cards.idea: A mixed question gives you a queue and a stack, and a list of moves between them. The queue always gives back its oldest item. The stack always gives back its newest. Combining the two lets you reverse order, rotate order, or build new output sequences.
cards.definition:
- **Queue to stack:** `x = dequeue(Q); push(S, x)`.
- **Stack to queue:** `x = pop(S); enqueue(Q, x)`.
- **Reverse a queue:** move all of Q onto S, then all of S back to Q.
- **Rotate a queue:** `enqueue(Q, dequeue(Q))`.
- **Output of a split:** if each arriving item is pushed on S or enqueued on Q, and then S is emptied before Q, the output is the S items in reverse arrival order followed by the Q items in arrival order.
cards.intuition_full: The two containers hold different 'orientations' of the same list. A queue keeps the arrival order along its length, oldest first. A stack keeps it reversed from the viewpoint of removal, newest first. Transferring items one at a time between them flips the removal order each time an item crosses. That is why a round trip through a stack reverses a queue: the first item to cross is the last to come back. Questions that assign every arriving item to the stack or the queue reduce to a clean rule: the output is a decreasing run (from the stack) followed by an increasing run (from the queue), when the arrivals are in increasing order. Count the assignments by trying every split point of the output sequence. For all of these, a tidy table with one line per operation prevents the usual slips.

examples.setup: A queue holds [2, 5, 8, 1] (front on the left). Move every item from the queue to an empty stack (dequeue then push). Then move every item from the stack back to the queue (pop then enqueue). What is the queue now?
steps: Queue Q = [2, 5, 8, 1], stack S empty. Rule: dequeue the front of Q, push it on S.
Move 2 and 5: S = [2, 5] (5 on top), Q = [8, 1].
Move 8 and 1: S = [2, 5, 8, 1] (1 on top), Q is empty.
Now pop S and enqueue: pop gives 1, then 8. Q = [1, 8], S = [2, 5].
Pop gives 5, then 2. Q = [1, 8, 5, 2].
examples.answer: The queue is [1, 8, 5, 2], the original order reversed. A stack reverses what passes through it; a queue keeps the order.

examples.setup: Elements 1, 2, 3, 4 arrive in this order. Each is placed either on a stack S (push) or in a queue Q (enqueue). Afterwards S is emptied by pops, and then Q is emptied by dequeues. How many assignments give the output `2 1 3 4`?
steps: The output is the S items in reverse arrival order (they pop newest first), followed by the Q items in arrival order.
So the output must be a decreasing run followed by an increasing run. Split `2 1 3 4` after k items.
k = 2: S gets {1, 2}: pops give 2, 1. Q gets {3, 4}: 3, 4. Output 2 1 3 4. Works.
k = 1: S gets {2}, Q gets {1, 3, 4}: output 2, then 1, 3, 4. Works.
k = 0: Q gets all four: output 1 2 3 4, not the target. k = 3: S holds {1, 2, 3} and pops 3, 2, 1, so the output would start with 3. Fails.
examples.answer: 2 assignments: S = {1, 2}, Q = {3, 4}; and S = {2}, Q = {1, 3, 4}. Stack output is reversed, queue output is in order.

cards.title: Queue applications
cards.simple: Think of a rumour spreading through a school. First the starter's friends hear it, then their friends, then friends of friends. A queue remembers who heard first, so those people pass it on first. That is breadth-first search: one level at a time. The same queue idea runs a circle game where every second child leaves, or a bus stop where people board in order. In exam words: BFS and level-order traversal use a queue as the frontier; Josephus-style elimination rotates a queue; schedulers keep ready queues.
cards.idea: Queues fit any job where the oldest waiting item should go next. **BFS** uses a queue for its frontier, so nodes are visited in order of distance, and **level-order** traversal of a tree is BFS. **Round-robin** scheduling and the **Josephus** circle rotate a queue, and printers and buffers keep first-come, first-served queues.
cards.definition:
- **BFS:** enqueue the start and mark it seen. While the queue is not empty: dequeue `u`, visit it; for each unseen neighbour `v`, mark it and enqueue it.
- **Level order:** BFS on a tree; each node's children are enqueued left to right.
- **Josephus (every k-th out):** repeat: rotate `k - 1` people from the front to the rear, then remove the next.
- **Round robin:** dequeue a process, run it for a time slice, enqueue it again if unfinished.
cards.intuition_full: Because the queue returns the oldest item, nodes discovered earlier are expanded earlier. All nodes at distance 1 are enqueued before any at distance 2, and so on. So the order of dequeuing is by non-decreasing distance. That is why BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs and why the queue size is the width of the current level. Marking a node as seen when it is enqueued keeps each node in the queue at most once. If you mark on dequeue, a node reachable by several edges can be enqueued several times. Josephus works by the same rule: a queue rotating by dequeue-and-enqueue holds a circle, and dropping an item after a rotation removes every k-th person. Level order of a tree has the same shape as BFS, with no seen flags needed since a tree has no cycles.

examples.setup: Run breadth-first search from A with a queue. Edges (directed): A to B, A to C, B to D, C to D, C to E. Mark a node seen when it is enqueued. In which order are nodes visited (dequeued)?
steps: Queue [A]. A is marked seen.
Dequeue A and visit it. Enqueue its unseen neighbours B, C. Queue [B, C].
Dequeue B, visit it. Enqueue D (unseen). Queue [C, D].
Dequeue C, visit it. D is already seen, so skip it. Enqueue E. Queue [D, E].
Dequeue D and E. They have no unseen neighbours. The queue is empty.
Visit order: A, B, C, D, E: all nodes at distance 1 from A before any at distance 2.
examples.answer: A, B, C, D, E. The queue makes the search finish one level before it starts the next.

examples.setup: Six people, numbered 1 to 6, stand in a queue (1 at the front). Repeat: the person at the front moves to the rear and stays; the next person is removed permanently. Who is left?

Move 3 to the rear, remove 4: [5, 6, 1, 3].
Move 5 to the rear, remove 6: [1, 3, 5].
Move 1 to the rear, remove 3: [5, 1].
Move 5 to the rear, remove 1: [5].
examples.answer: Person 5 is left. This is the Josephus problem with every second person removed: a queue where the front is rotated to the rear, then the next is dropped.

examples.setup: Run the same BFS but mark a node seen only when it is **dequeued**, and enqueue every neighbour. How often is D dequeued?
steps: Queue [A]. Dequeue A, enqueue B and C: [B, C].
Dequeue B, enqueue D: [C, D].
Dequeue C. Enqueue D and E, even though D is already in the queue: [D, D, E].
D is in the queue twice, so it is dequeued twice (the second time it must be skipped using the seen flag).
examples.answer: D is dequeued twice. Marking at dequeue time lets the queue hold duplicates (up to one per edge), so mark at enqueue time to keep it to one copy per node.

cards.title: Python deque
cards.simple: Python's ordinary list is great at its right end, but slow at its left end: removing the first item makes every other item shuffle one place. The `deque` in the `collections` module is built for both ends. Adding or removing at the left or at the right is quick. So when you need a queue in Python, reach for a deque, not a list. In exam words: `collections.deque` gives O(1) `append`, `appendleft`, `pop` and `popleft`; `list.pop(0)` is O(n).
cards.idea: A **deque** in Python is a double-ended queue from the `collections` module. Both ends support O(1) insertion and removal. A plain list is fast only at its right end, so using `list.pop(0)` for a queue makes every removal linear.
cards.definition:
`from collections import deque`

- `d.append(x)`, `d.pop()`: right end.
- `d.appendleft(x)`, `d.popleft()`: left end.
- `d.rotate(k)`: rotate right by `k` (left if `k` is negative).
- `d[i]`: index access, O(1) near the ends but O(n) in the middle.
- `deque(iterable, maxlen=m)`: bounded deque; appending past `m` drops from the opposite end.

Costs: all four end operations O(1). `list.pop(0)` and `list.insert(0, x)` are O(n).
cards.intuition_full: Underneath, a deque is a chain of small blocks, with pointers to the first and last block. Taking an item from either end touches only the end block, so no other item moves. A list is one contiguous block, so removing the front leaves a hole at index 0 that must be closed by shifting everything. This is the same cost that arrays have in the arrays chapter: access by index is fast, but changes at the front are slow. The price of the deque is the middle: `d[500]` must walk blocks, so indexing deep inside is slower than for a list. Typical uses: queues for BFS, sliding windows, and keeping the last `m` items with `maxlen`. In an exam, the question is usually which operation is O(1) and what the contents are after a short sequence.

examples.setup:
What does this print?
```python
from collections import deque
d = deque([5, 6, 7])
d.append(8)
d.appendleft(4)
d.pop()
d.popleft()
print(d[0], len(d))
```
steps: `append(8)` adds at the right end: [5, 6, 7, 8].
`appendleft(4)` adds at the left end: [4, 5, 6, 7, 8].
`pop()` removes from the right end (8): [4, 5, 6, 7].
`popleft()` removes from the left end (4): [5, 6, 7].
`d[0]` is the first item, 5, and `len(d)` is 3.
examples.answer: It prints `5 3`. `pop` and `append` work at the right end; `popleft` and `appendleft` work at the left end. All four are O(1).

examples.setup: A breadth-first search over a graph processes 1000 queued vertices and takes each from the front of the queue. Compare the total cost of the removals when the queue is a Python list with `pop(0)` and when it is a `deque` with `popleft()`. Count element moves in the worst case.
steps: With a list of size k, `pop(0)` moves the k - 1 remaining items one place left.
If the list is 1000 items long and shrinks by one each call, the moves are 999 + 998 + ... + 1 + 0 = 1000 x 999 / 2 = 499,500.
With a deque, `popleft()` moves no items: 0 moves, each call O(1).
So the list version costs Theta(n^2) just for the removals, and the deque version Theta(n).
examples.answer: 499,500 element moves for the list, none for the deque. In Python, use `collections.deque` for a queue; `list.pop(0)` is O(n).

examples.setup:
What are the contents of the deque after each step?
```python
from collections import deque
d = deque([1, 2, 3], maxlen=3)
d.append(4)
d.appendleft(0)
```
steps: `maxlen=3` means the deque never holds more than 3 items. It starts as [1, 2, 3].
`append(4)` would make 4 items, so the item at the **opposite** end (the left one, 1) is dropped: [2, 3, 4].
`appendleft(0)` also exceeds the limit, so the item at the right end (4) is dropped: [0, 2, 3].
examples.answer: [2, 3, 4] and then [0, 2, 3]. With `maxlen`, adding at one end silently discards from the other end.

cards.what_full:
A **deque** in Python is a double-ended queue from the `collections` module. Both ends support O(1) insertion and removal. A plain list is fast only at its right end, so using `list.pop(0)` for a queue makes every removal linear.

`from collections import deque`

- `d.append(x)`, `d.pop()`: right end.
- `d.appendleft(x)`, `d.popleft()`: left end.
- `d.rotate(k)`: rotate right by `k` (left if `k` is negative).
- `d[i]`: index access, O(1) near the ends but O(n) in the middle.
- `deque(iterable, maxlen=m)`: bounded deque; appending past `m` drops from the opposite end.

Costs: all four end operations O(1). `list.pop(0)` and `list.insert(0, x)` are O(n).

**Worked example.** What does this print?
```python
from collections import deque
d = deque([5, 6, 7])
d.append(8)
d.appendleft(4)
d.pop()
d.popleft()
print(d[0], len(d))
```

1. `deque([5, 6, 7])` holds [5, 6, 7].
2. `append(8)` adds at the right end: [5, 6, 7, 8].
3. `appendleft(4)` adds at the left end: [4, 5, 6, 7, 8].
4. `pop()` removes from the right end (8): [4, 5, 6, 7].
5. `popleft()` removes from the left end (4): [5, 6, 7].
6. `d[0]` is the first item, 5, and `len(d)` is 3.

**Answer:** It prints `5 3`. `pop` and `append` work at the right end; `popleft` and `appendleft` work at the left end. All four are O(1).

scenes.title: Circular queue of 6 cells: rear wraps to index 0

objects.text: front = first item,  rear = next free slot

steps.caption: Let the indices wrap. Empty when `front == rear`. Full when `(rear + 1) mod 6 == front`. Start: `front = 0`, `rear = 0`.
Enqueue A to E stores them at indices 0 to 4. `rear` moves to 5. Now `(5 + 1) mod 6 = 0 = front`, so the queue is full with 5 items. Capacity is n - 1 = 5.

Enqueue G goes to index 0. `rear = 1`. Now `(1 + 1) mod 6 = 2 = front`: full again.
Items from front to rear are C, D, E, F, G. Count = `(rear - front + 6) mod 6 = (1 - 2 + 6) mod 6 = 5`.

scenes.title: Linked queue: head and tail pointers

steps.caption: Follow head and tail. Empty queue: `head = tail = NULL`. `enqueue(5)` creates a node. Both `head` and `tail` point at it.

`enqueue(2)`: the same two assignments. List 5 → 8 → 2, `head` at 5, `tail` at 2.
`dequeue()`: return `head.value` (5), then `head = head.next`. The 5 node is unlinked and `head` is at 8.
`dequeue()` returns 8 and `head` moves to 2. The last `dequeue()` returns 2 and `head` becomes NULL. Now the queue is empty, so `tail` must also be set to NULL.

steps.caption: Work both ends. `insertFirst(7)`: the deque is [7].

scenes.title: Stack from two queues: reach the newest item

steps.caption: Reach the newest item. Three pushes enqueue 4, 7, 2 on the active queue: [4, 7, 2]. The newest item, 2, sits at the rear.

scenes.title: list.pop(0) shifts everything; a deque moves a pointer

steps.caption: Remove from the front five times. `pop(0)` removes the first element, and every element after it moves one place left. The list has 5 items, so 4 shifts.

Next: 3 items remain, 2 shifts.
Next: 2 items remain, 1 shift.
Last: 1 item remains, 0 shifts. Total = 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 10.
A deque only moves its front pointer: 0 shifts. In general the list needs n(n - 1)/2 shifts for n removals.
